prompt: A ReportService queries the database, renders a PDF, and emails it to stakeholders. Which principle does it most directly violate?
options: Single Responsibility
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
Open/Closed
explanation: It has three reasons to change (data access, rendering, delivery) that are owned by different concerns. Split it into a repository, a renderer and a notifier, then compose them.

prompt: Square inherits from Rectangle, and setting Width on a Square also changes its Height. Code that sets width = 5, height = 4 and expects area 20 breaks. Which principle is violated?
options: Single Responsibility
Liskov Substitution
Interface Segregation
Dependency Inversion
explanation: A subtype must honor the base type's contract: here, that width and height can be set independently. Square strengthens the invariant, so it can't be substituted for Rectangle. "Is-a" in the real world doesn't guarantee behavioral subtyping.

prompt: Adding a new payment method means editing a switch(paymentType) statement in six classes. Which refactor best satisfies Open/Closed?
options: Move all six switches into one static PaymentHelper class
Add an IPaymentMethod implementation per type, resolved via DI
Replace the PaymentType enum with string constants from config
Add a default branch to each switch that throws NotSupported
explanation: Replace the conditional with polymorphism: each type's behavior lives in its own class, and a new type means adding a class and registering it, with no edits to existing code. Centralizing the switch reduces duplication, but you still modify it for every new type.

prompt: You want to add caching around an IProductRepository without changing its implementation or its callers. Which pattern fits?
options: Decorator
Adapter
Factory Method
Observer
explanation: A Decorator implements the same interface, wraps the inner instance, and adds behavior before or after delegating. CachedProductRepository : IProductRepository wraps the real one. Adapter is different: it changes an interface to match another one.

prompt: The ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline (and Angular HTTP interceptors) is closest to which pattern?
options: Chain of Responsibility
Template Method pattern
Mediator with handlers
Composite of handlers
explanation: Each handler gets the request and decides whether to handle it, short-circuit it, or call next() to pass it along the chain. Order matters: auth must come before endpoints, and exception handling comes first.

prompt: What is the strongest argument against a classic static Singleton (private constructor, static Instance) in a modern .NET or Angular codebase?
options: Hidden global state and a hard-wired concrete dependency
It can't be made thread-safe without one global lock
It always leaks memory, since the instance is never freed
Static access is noticeably slower than instance method calls
explanation: Consumers reach for Singleton.Instance instead of declaring a dependency, so you can't swap in a fake and state leaks between tests. You still get a single instance by registering a singleton lifetime in the DI container (AddSingleton, providedIn: 'root').

prompt: What is the main reason behind "favor composition over inheritance"?
options: Subclasses couple to the parent's internals, so base changes break them
Inheritance adds virtual-call overhead that composition avoids entirely
Composition lets a C# class inherit behavior from several base classes
Composed objects use less memory than deep inheritance hierarchies do
explanation: This is the fragile base class problem: subclasses depend on how the parent calls its own methods. Composition depends only on a collaborator's public contract, and you can swap that collaborator at runtime. It is not a performance argument: virtual dispatch and an extra object reference cost about the same either way.

prompt: An Order aggregate exposes `public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; }`. Why is this an encapsulation problem even though there is no setter?
options: Callers can still Add/Remove lines, bypassing invariants like Total
It should be a public field, since properties add needless overhead
List<T> can't be serialized, so the aggregate can't be persisted
Nothing: with no setter, the collection is effectively immutable
explanation: Getter-only protects the reference, not the contents. Expose IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> (backed by a private list, ideally via AsReadOnly()) plus intention-revealing methods like AddLine(), which enforce the rules. Fields vs properties isn't the issue: a public field would be even worse.

prompt: In C#, a base-class constructor calls a virtual method that the derived class overrides. What happens?
options: The derived override runs before the derived constructor body does
The base implementation runs, since the derived part isn't built yet
It throws InvalidOperationException at runtime during construction
It fails to compile, because constructors can't make virtual calls
explanation: The object's runtime type is the derived type from the start, so virtual dispatch reaches the override. Derived field initializers have run, but the derived constructor body hasn't. Nothing throws: it compiles and runs with half-initialized state, which is why analyzers flag virtual calls in constructors (CA2214). C++ behaves differently and dispatches to the base.

prompt: What does the Dependency Inversion Principle state?
options: High-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete modules
Every class must be resolved from a DI container, never new-ed
Low-level modules should construct the dependencies they need
Every concrete class needs a matching interface for testability
explanation: Policy code (for example OrderService) owns an abstraction (IOrderRepository) that the infrastructure implements. DI containers are a mechanism for wiring this up; DIP is the design rule, and it doesn't mean adding an interface for every class.

prompt: In ASP.NET Core, a Singleton service takes a Scoped DbContext in its constructor. What is the problem?
options: A captive dependency: one DbContext is shared across all requests
Nothing: the container still creates a new DbContext per request
The DbContext silently becomes transient inside the singleton
It only matters in unit tests, where no request scope is created
explanation: A longer-lived service captures a shorter-lived one. DbContext isn't thread-safe and its change tracker grows forever. Scope validation (on by default in Development) throws at startup. Fixes: inject IServiceScopeFactory or IDbContextFactory, or make the consumer scoped.

prompt: An Angular service uses @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }), and the same service is also listed in a lazy-loaded route's `providers`. What do components in that route get?
options: The root singleton, because route-level providers are ignored
A separate instance from the lazy route's environment injector
A compile-time error for providing the same service twice
A fresh instance for every component that injects the service
explanation: Lazy routes with providers create a child environment injector. Resolution walks up from the nearest injector, so the route's provider shadows root. That's useful for feature-scoped state, but it's a classic source of "why is my state not shared?" bugs.

prompt: A Stack<T> class inherits from List<T> to reuse its storage. What's the main design problem?
options: Callers inherit Insert/RemoveAt and can break the LIFO invariant
It's slower than a stack written directly over a raw array
It won't compile, because List<T> is a sealed class in .NET
Nothing: a stack is a list, so this is a valid is-a relationship
explanation: Inheritance brings the parent's whole public surface. Java's Stack extends Vector is the famous example: you can insert into the middle of a stack. Wrapping a private List<T> and exposing only Push/Pop/Peek keeps the invariant. Speed isn't the issue, and List<T> isn't sealed, so it compiles.

prompt: In TypeScript: class Cart { readonly items: Item[] = []; } What happens with cart.items.push(item) from outside the class?
options: Compile error: items is readonly, so the push call is rejected
It compiles and mutates: readonly only blocks reassigning items
It throws a TypeError at runtime, because the array is frozen
It compiles, but push is silently ignored on readonly members
explanation: The readonly modifier applies to the property binding, not the array. To block mutation through the type, declare items: readonly Item[] (or ReadonlyArray<Item>) and change it through methods like addItem(). Nothing is frozen at runtime unless you call Object.freeze.

prompt: An aggregate exposes public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines; where _lines is a private List<OrderLine>. A caller writes ((List<OrderLine>)order.Lines).Add(line). What's the best fix?
options: Make _lines a readonly field so its contents can't be changed
Return a cached _lines.AsReadOnly() wrapper instead of the list
Expose it as IEnumerable<OrderLine>, which has no Add method at all
Mark Lines as virtual so derived classes can guard any writes
explanation: An interface type is only a compile-time hint; if the object is really your List<T>, a cast exposes it. ReadOnlyCollection<T> wraps the list: casting it to List<T> throws InvalidCastException, and Add via IList<T> throws NotSupportedException. A readonly field only protects the reference, and IEnumerable<T> has the same cast hole.

prompt: You must log every call made through an IPaymentGateway, without editing the concrete gateway or any of its callers. Which approach fits best?
options: An abstract factory that chooses between several gateway implementations
A Template Method base class that every gateway subclass must inherit from
A static Logger singleton that each caller invokes before using the gateway
A Decorator implementing IPaymentGateway that logs and delegates to the inner one
explanation: A Decorator has the same interface and wraps the real gateway, so callers and the concrete class stay untouched; with DI you swap the registration. A factory only decides which type to create, Template Method would force edits to the gateway's hierarchy, and a static logger requires changing every caller.

prompt: An Angular HttpInterceptorFn can answer a request from cache and never call next(). Why does this make Template Method the wrong description of interceptors?
options: Template Method cannot be used with functions, only with classes
Links are composed at runtime and each one may stop the flow, with no base class fixing the steps
Interceptors always run in a random order, while Template Method requires a fixed one
Template Method only applies to server code, not to code running in a browser
explanation: Template Method fixes the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses fill in hooks. Interceptors are separate links assembled at runtime, and each decides whether to call next(), which is Chain of Responsibility. Their order is deterministic (registration order), and the pattern has nothing to do with where code runs.

prompt: ReadOnlyCollection<T> implements IList<T> but throws NotSupportedException from Add. Callers who accept an IList<T> and call Add now crash. Which principle does this break?
options: Interface Segregation, because the interface has too many methods
Single Responsibility, because the list both stores and protects items
Liskov Substitution, because the subtype can't honor the base contract
Dependency Inversion, because callers depend on an interface not a class
explanation: Callers written against IList<T> are entitled to call Add, and the subtype breaks that expectation, which is LSP. ISP is the tempting second answer (the wide interface is what invites the wart), but the symptom described, a substitute that misbehaves, is LSP. Depending on an interface is what DIP recommends, not a violation of it.

prompt: A ReportExporter has a switch on format (Pdf, Csv, Xlsx). Each new format means editing it, and tests for old formats must be re-run. What best applies Open/Closed?
options: Wrap the switch in try/catch and log unknown formats instead of failing
Add one IReportFormat implementation per format and resolve it by key via DI
Move the switch into a static helper so ReportExporter itself never changes
Make ReportExporter abstract and subclass it once per combination of format
explanation: OCP means new behavior is added as new code, not by editing tested code. One IReportFormat per format, resolved through DI, does that. Moving the switch to a helper just relocates the edits, catching unknown formats only changes how failure looks, and subclassing the exporter per format multiplies classes while still coupling creation to the type.

prompt: CartService is providedIn root. A component lists CartService in its own `providers` array. How do its child components resolve CartService?
options: They get the root singleton, because component providers are ignored
They get a new instance per child, created each time they inject it
They get the parent component's instance, shadowing the root singleton
They fail at build time, since two providers for one token conflict
explanation: Component-level providers create an instance bound to that component's element injector, and everything beneath it resolves to that nearest provider before reaching root. Children share the parent's one instance (not one each), and the rest of the app keeps the root one. Providing a token at several levels is legal, so there is no conflict error.
